blindSummary:
This is a high-danger environment for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the colonial-era penal code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a cash bribe of about fifty dollars in a coastal city, and 25 trans and intersex people told a foreign broadcaster this kind of police harassment is "common." The national human-rights commission's year-long report on violence against sexual and gender minorities documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist was murdered (his body was found packed in a metal box) — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, this country's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The high court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a transgender-protection rights bill). In May 2026, the high court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The supreme court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and an appellate court ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. Thousands of gay travellers reportedly visit annually through specialised tour operators.

There is no anti-discrimination law and no legal-gender-recognition procedure yet, but the court-ordered transgender-protection bill is a positive trajectory.
blindOutOfScope: Terrorism risks near one of the country's border regions, general crime, and political instability affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: A foreign home ministry's official country-of-origin guidance on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression here (Feb 2025, updated July 2026): assessment used in asylum claims - legal position, societal treatment, state protection.

A foreign broadcaster's investigation: how trans and intersex people survive in this country - 'forced to pay bribes at every step'; a young trans woman describes being arrested on a pretext by police in a coastal city and held until she paid a cash bribe of about fifty dollars; trans people use male pseudonyms for safety; police extortion is systemic.

NOTE: the national human-rights commission's year-long report on violence and discrimination against sexual and gender minorities here (Sept 2025) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

National human-rights commission press release (Aug 2025): the high court, sitting in a regional city, affirmed legal recognition of transgender people in this country and directed the state to enact transgender-protection rights legislation, ruling that prisons do not protect trans people's dignity and privacy; the case arose from invasive, nonconsensual medical procedures on a trans woman during incarceration after a 'personation' arrest.
Trans-advocacy knowledge-portal article: this country's high court rules there is a constitutional right to legal gender recognition - analysis of the landmark decision.
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying newswire report (Dec 2024) covers a man sentenced to 50 years in jail in this country for killing an LGBTQ activist.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): progress largely through courts - forced anal testing ruled unconstitutional (2018, compensation awarded 2024); the supreme court upheld LGBTQ organisations' freedom to register (2023), followed by pushback including protests and homophobic remarks by religious and political leaders; a 2024 high-court temporary order against incitement to hatred; same-sex conduct remains criminalised and no legal gender recognition.

National daily (Sept 2025): coverage of the national human-rights commission's year-long report - 682 cases of harassment documented across regions (50 sexual harassment, 100 verbal abuse); queer residents face eviction, online trolling, and being waylaid by organised groups who strip and violate them; the country is 'deeply socially conservative'.

A foreign government's 2010 human-rights report on this country: documents the 2007-08 post-election violence (~1,150 killed), security-force abuses, mob violence, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation under the penal code and societal discrimination.
blindLocalsOnly: The court-ordered transgender-protection rights bill and the 2026 legal-gender-recognition ruling are resident-facing developments; the eviction/arrest/mob-violence toll falls on residents.
blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, applies to tourists) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
